subtitle: Step through 10 turning points across the Greek world—from Minoan Crete, the alphabet, and the 776 BC Olympics to Athenian democracy, Marathon, Salamis, the Parthenon, and Alexander.

milestones.title: Minoan Palaces on Crete & Mycenaean Lion Gate
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which island home of Knossos palace inspired the Greek myth of King Minos and the Minotaur?
milestones.imageCaption: Reconstructed red columns and courtyard walls at the Bronze Age Minoan palace of Knossos on Crete.
milestones.catalyst: Centuries before Classical Athens, seafaring Minoans on the island of Crete painted dolphin frescoes at Knossos, while mainland Mycenaean warrior-kings built giant stone citadels remembered in stories of the Trojan War.
milestones.turningPoint: Island children watched painted cargo ships unload copper, olive oil jars, and colourful pottery in Cretan harbours.
milestones.impact: Gave later Greeks heroic legends of King Minos, the Minotaur’s Labyrinth, Achilles, and Odysseus!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 800 BC): Rise of Independent City-States (Poleis) & The Greek Alphabet.

ks2.story: Centuries before Classical Athens, seafaring Minoans on the island of Crete painted dolphin frescoes at Knossos, while mainland Mycenaean warrior-kings built giant stone citadels remembered in stories of the Trojan War.
ks2.significance: Gave later Greeks heroic legends of King Minos, the Minotaur’s Labyrinth, Achilles, and Odysseus!
ks2.childrenLife: Island children watched painted cargo ships unload copper, olive oil jars, and colourful pottery in Cretan harbours.
ks2.quote: “Knossos palace had so many winding storerooms and courtyards that later Greeks imagined the myth of the Labyrinth!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Which island home of Knossos palace inspired the Greek myth of King Minos and the Minotaur?

milestones.title: Rise of Independent City-States (Poleis) & The Greek Alphabet
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which two Greek letters give us our modern English word "alphabet"?
milestones.imageCaption: Ancient Greek letters carved cleanly into marble, including dedicated letters for vowel sounds.
milestones.catalyst: Separated by steep mountains and linked by the Aegean Sea, independent city-states (poleis) grew around high Acropolis forts and Agora markets—and adapted Phoenician script by adding vowels to write Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey!
milestones.turningPoint: Boys practised scratching the 24 Greek letters onto reusable wooden boards coated in smooth beeswax.
milestones.impact: Our English word "alphabet" comes straight from Greece’s first two letters: Alpha (Α) and Beta (Β)!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (776 BC): First Recorded Ancient Olympic Games & Sacred Truce.

ks2.story: Separated by steep mountains and linked by the Aegean Sea, independent city-states (poleis) grew around high Acropolis forts and Agora markets—and adapted Phoenician script by adding vowels to write Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey!
ks2.significance: Our English word "alphabet" comes straight from Greece’s first two letters: Alpha (Α) and Beta (Β)!
ks2.childrenLife: Boys practised scratching the 24 Greek letters onto reusable wooden boards coated in smooth beeswax.
ks2.quote: “Adding vowel letters (A, E, I, O, U) meant anyone could sound out Greek poetry, laws, and names accurately!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Which two Greek letters give us our modern English word "alphabet"?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Alpha and Beta—the first two letters of the Greek alphabet!

milestones.title: First Recorded Ancient Olympic Games & Sacred Truce
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What did the Sacred Olympic Truce (ekecheiria) guarantee every four years?
milestones.imageCaption: The vaulted stone entrance and 192-metre ancient running track (stadion) at Olympia in southern Greece.
milestones.catalyst: Every four years in honour of Zeus at Olympia, heralds announced a Sacred Truce pausing wars across Greece so athletes could race the 192m stadion, throw discus and javelin, wrestle, and race four-horse chariots.
milestones.turningPoint: Young spectators camped in tents around Olympia watching jugglers, poets, and barefoot sprinters.
milestones.impact: United rival city-states in shared Greek religion and sport—and later saw Spartan princess Cynisca win Olympic chariot crowns in 396 BC!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (508 BC): Athens Launches Direct Democracy on the Pnyx Hill.

ks2.story: Every four years in honour of Zeus at Olympia, heralds announced a Sacred Truce pausing wars across Greece so athletes could race the 192m stadion, throw discus and javelin, wrestle, and race four-horse chariots.

ks2.childrenLife: Young spectators camped in tents around Olympia watching jugglers, poets, and barefoot sprinters.
ks2.quote: “Olympic champions won no gold or silver medals—their prize was a sacred wreath of wild olive leaves!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What did the Sacred Olympic Truce (ekecheiria) guarantee every four years?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Warring Greek city-states paused fighting so athletes and visitors could travel safely to and from Olympia!

milestones.title: Athens Launches Direct Democracy on the Pnyx Hill
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which three large groups living in Athens were NOT allowed to vote in the Assembly?
milestones.imageCaption: Carved stone speaker’s platform (bema) on the Pnyx hill in Athens where citizens debated and voted.
milestones.catalyst: Reformer Cleisthenes reorganised Athens under demokratia ("rule by the people"): 6,000 adult male citizens met on the Pnyx hill to debate and vote directly by raising hands—unlike military Sparta ruled by two kings and elders!
milestones.turningPoint: In Athens boys learned reading and lyre music while girls wove indoors; in rival Sparta boys entered agoge barracks at seven and girls trained in athletics!
milestones.impact: Planted the seed of modern democracy and citizen juries—though Athens excluded women, foreign metics, and enslaved people.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (490 BC): Hoplite Phalanx Victory at the Battle of Marathon.

ks2.significance: Planted the seed of modern democracy and citizen juries—though Athens excluded women, foreign metics, and enslaved people.
ks2.childrenLife: In Athens boys learned reading and lyre music while girls wove indoors; in rival Sparta boys entered agoge barracks at seven and girls trained in athletics!
ks2.quote: “Once a year Athenians could scratch a power-hungry politician’s name onto a pot shard (ostrakon) to banish him for ten years!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Which three large groups living in Athens were NOT allowed to vote in the Assembly?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: All women, foreign-born residents (metics), and enslaved people!

milestones.title: Hoplite Phalanx Victory at the Battle of Marathon
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why is a modern 26.2-mile long-distance race called a "marathon"?
milestones.imageCaption: Painted Greek vase showing bronze-helmeted hoplite warriors locking round shields and thrusting spears.
milestones.provenance: Archaeological Museum Collection / Public Domain (Wikimedia Commons)
milestones.catalyst: When Persian King Darius sent an invasion fleet to beach at Marathon, 10,000 heavily armoured Athenian and Plataean hoplites locked bronze shields in a tight phalanx and charged at a run to defeat the larger Persian force!
milestones.turningPoint: Athenian families cheered with relief when word arrived from Marathon before the Persian ships could sail round to the city.
milestones.impact: Saved young Athenian democracy and inspired the modern 26.2-mile marathon race named after messenger Pheidippides!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (480 BC): Thermopylae’s Pass & Trireme Victory at Salamis.

ks2.story: When Persian King Darius sent an invasion fleet to beach at Marathon, 10,000 heavily armoured Athenian and Plataean hoplites locked bronze shields in a tight phalanx and charged at a run to defeat the larger Persian force!
ks2.significance: Saved young Athenian democracy and inspired the modern 26.2-mile marathon race named after messenger Pheidippides!
ks2.childrenLife: Athenian families cheered with relief when word arrived from Marathon before the Persian ships could sail round to the city.
ks2.quote: “Each hoplite’s round shield protected his own left side and his neighbour’s right—teamwork kept the phalanx unbroken!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why is a modern 26.2-mile long-distance race called a "marathon"?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: In memory of the messenger run from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens (and Pheidippides’ epic runs in 490 BC)!

milestones.title: Thermopylae’s Pass & Trireme Victory at Salamis
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did narrow geography help the outnumbered Greeks at BOTH Thermopylae and Salamis?
milestones.imageCaption: Full-scale sea-going reconstruction of an Athenian three-banked wooden trireme warship (Olympias).
milestones.provenance: Hellenic Navy / Photograph via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)
milestones.catalyst: After Spartan King Leonidas, 300 Spartans, and Greek allies held King Xerxes’ vast army for three days at narrow Thermopylae, Athenian commander Themistocles lured Persia’s fleet into the tight Straits of Salamis and smashed it with agile bronze-rammed triremes!
milestones.turningPoint: Evacuated Athenian families watched from nearby islands as 170-oar Greek triremes turned the tide in the narrow strait.
milestones.impact: Kept Greek city-states independent and ushered in the Classical Golden Age of fifth-century BC Athens.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (447–432 BC): Pericles & Phidias Build the Marble Parthenon.

ks2.story: After Spartan King Leonidas, 300 Spartans, and Greek allies held King Xerxes’ vast army for three days at narrow Thermopylae, Athenian commander Themistocles lured Persia’s fleet into the tight Straits of Salamis and smashed it with agile bronze-rammed triremes!
ks2.significance: Kept Greek city-states independent and ushered in the Classical Golden Age of fifth-century BC Athens.
ks2.childrenLife: Evacuated Athenian families watched from nearby islands as 170-oar Greek triremes turned the tide in the narrow strait.
ks2.quote: “Powered by 170 free rowers pulling three tiers of oars, a Greek trireme turned like an athlete to strike with its bronze ram!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How did narrow geography help the outnumbered Greeks at BOTH Thermopylae and Salamis?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Narrow mountain walls and narrow sea straits stopped Persia’s much larger army and fleet surrounding the Greeks all at once!

milestones.title: Pericles & Phidias Build the Marble Parthenon
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How can you spot the difference between Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian column tops (capitals)?
milestones.imageCaption: Fluted marble Doric columns of the Parthenon temple dedicated to Athena high on the Acropolis of Athens.
milestones.catalyst: Led by statesman Pericles and master sculptor Phidias, masons raised the gleaming marble Parthenon atop the Acropolis—housing a 12-metre gold-and-ivory statue of patron goddess Athena.
milestones.turningPoint: Every four years Athenian families climbed the Acropolis in a joyful procession bringing Athena a freshly woven saffron robe!
milestones.impact: Set the blueprint for Classical Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian architecture copied on public buildings right across the world.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 430–350 BC): Open-Air Theatre Plus Socrates, Plato & Aristotle.

ks2.significance: Set the blueprint for Classical Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian architecture copied on public buildings right across the world.
ks2.childrenLife: Every four years Athenian families climbed the Acropolis in a joyful procession bringing Athena a freshly woven saffron robe!
ks2.quote: “Look closely at museums, courts, and town halls in Britain—their stone columns echo the Acropolis of Athens!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How can you spot the difference between Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian column tops (capitals)?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Doric is plain and sturdy, Ionic has curled ram-horn scrolls, and Corinthian is carved with leafy acanthus plants!

milestones.title: Open-Air Theatre Plus Socrates, Plato & Aristotle
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Ancient Greek actors wear large sculpted masks with wide mouths on stage?
milestones.imageCaption: The semi-circular limestone theatre of Epidaurus, seating 14,000 spectators with crystal-clear acoustics.
milestones.catalyst: Fourteen thousand citizens packed semi-circular hillside theatres to watch masked tragedies and comedies, while philosophers Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle walked Athens asking sharp questions about justice, logic, and nature.
milestones.turningPoint: Even from the highest stone row of Epidaurus theatre, listeners could hear a coin drop or paper rustle on stage below!
milestones.impact: Gave the world live drama ("theatre", "tragedy", "comedy", "scene") and scientific classification.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 400 BC): Hippocrates of Kos & Natural Medical Observation.

ks2.story: Fourteen thousand citizens packed semi-circular hillside theatres to watch masked tragedies and comedies, while philosophers Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle walked Athens asking sharp questions about justice, logic, and nature.
ks2.significance: Gave the world live drama ("theatre", "tragedy", "comedy", "scene") and scientific classification.
ks2.childrenLife: Even from the highest stone row of Epidaurus theatre, listeners could hear a coin drop or paper rustle on stage below!
ks2.quote: “Philosophy literally means ‘love of wisdom’ in Greek—never stop asking ‘Why?’ and testing your answers!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did Ancient Greek actors wear large sculpted masks with wide mouths on stage?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: So three actors could switch between many characters (old, young, sad, funny) visible from the back rows of huge outdoor theatres!

milestones.title: Hippocrates of Kos & Natural Medical Observation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Hippocrates change the way doctors explained and treated sickness?
milestones.imageCaption: Roman marble bust inscribed in Greek with the name of physician Hippocrates of Kos.
milestones.provenance: Archaeological Museum of Ostia / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)
milestones.catalyst: On the island of Kos, physician Hippocrates taught doctors to stop blaming every fever on angry gods—and instead examine the patient carefully, record daily symptoms, keep wounds clean, and prescribe rest and healthy food.
milestones.turningPoint: Medical apprentices learned to listen to breathing, check skin temperature, and write honest case notes.
milestones.impact: Earned Hippocrates the title "Father of Medicine" and inspired the ethical Hippocratic Oath protecting patients.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (336–146 BC & 1896): Alexander the Great, Library of Alexandria & Modern Legacy.

ks2.childrenLife: Medical apprentices learned to listen to breathing, check skin temperature, and write honest case notes.
ks2.quote: “First, do no harm—care for every sick patient honestly and keep their secrets safe.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How did Hippocrates change the way doctors explained and treated sickness?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: He taught that illnesses had natural causes in the body and environment, so doctors should observe symptoms carefully!

milestones.title: Alexander the Great, Library of Alexandria & Modern Legacy
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Name three things in modern life today that come directly from Ancient Greece.
milestones.imageCaption: Ancient Roman floor mosaic from Pompeii showing young King Alexander the Great riding his horse Bucephalus.
milestones.provenance: Naples National Archaeological Museum / Public Domain (Wikimedia Commons)
milestones.catalyst: Tutored by Aristotle, young King Alexander of Macedon spread Greek language and cities from Egypt to northwest India, sparking Alexandria’s Great Library (Euclid & Archimedes). Even after Rome conquered Greece in 146 BC, Greek culture lived on—reviving the modern Olympics in Athens in 1896!
milestones.turningPoint: In 1896 crowds filled Athens’ marble Panathenaic Stadium to cheer the very first modern international Olympic Games!
milestones.impact: Explains why Greek words, geometry, theatre, democracy, and the Olympic Games still shape life across the globe today.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes all 10 turning points in Ancient Greece (c. 1600–146 BC & Legacy).

ks2.quote: “Rome conquered Greek lands with legions in 146 BC—yet Greek art, science, and poetry captivated Rome and the modern world!”

ks2.detectiveAnswer: Democratic voting & juries, thousands of Greek-root English words (like school, dinosaur, galaxy), Classical columns, theatre, geometry, and the Olympic Games!
